title: Design a Multi-Region Session & Token Revocation Service
prompt: Design a globally distributed session and JWT revocation service for 100M active users across 4 regions. Edge API gateways handle 2M auth checks/sec and must validate tokens with < 2 ms p99 overhead, while security-critical revocations (password reset, compromised device, admin force-logout) must propagate globally within 5 seconds—even during cross-region network partitions or cache-node failures.

spark.summary: Pair short-lived stateless JWTs (5–15 min TTL) with an in-memory edge revocation filter, an authoritative multi-region session store, and async cross-region push invalidation with bounded retries and DLQ.
spark.keyTakeaway: If latency budgets leave no room for synchronous retries, never make synchronous cross-region database calls on every API request; keep the hot read path in edge memory and bound the revocation window with short JWT TTLs + fast push invalidation.
spark.byteSummary:
Purely stateless JWTs cannot be revoked before expiry, while purely stateful session lookups across 2M RPS/sec bottleneck on centralized Redis/DB latency. A production multi-region revocation architecture combines short-lived access tokens (`5–10 min` TTL) with a compact, two-tier revocation check at every regional Edge Gateway.

On the hot read path (`< 2 ms` p99), each Edge Gateway verifies the JWT signature locally using cached JWKS keys and checks `(jti, user_id, session_epoch)` against an in-memory revocation filter (e.g., compact hash set / Bloom + regional Redis fallback). Only revoked tokens or epoch-bumped users need entries, keeping memory footprint small because entries expire automatically when the JWT's `exp` passes.

On the write path, a Revocation API writes durably to the authoritative session store (e.g., multi-region DynamoDB/Spanner) and publishes an invalidation event to a cross-region replication stream. Regional fan-out workers update local Redis caches and push deltas to edge gateway memory within 1–3 seconds, routing any failed regional deliveries through bounded exponential backoff and a Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) with reconciliation polling.

learningJourney.title: Read/Write Asymmetry & Revocation Memory Footprint
learningJourney.purpose: Size the 2M RPS read path and bounded revocation set so edge memory stays tiny and predictable.

explanation.foundation: - **Read Path**: 2M auth checks/sec globally (~500K RPS/region) at `< 2 ms` p99.
explanation.core: - **Write Path**: ~1,000–5,000 revocations/sec (logouts, password resets, risk triggers).
explanation.deepDive: - **Bounded State**: With a 10-minute access token TTL, even 5,000 revocations/sec produces at most `5,000 × 600 = 3M` active deny entries (~100 MB in compact hash/Redis memory) before TTL eviction.

learningJourney.title: Short-Lived Access Tokens + User Session Epoch
learningJourney.purpose: Support both single-session logout (`jti`) and global 'log out all devices' (`epoch`) without storing every active token.

explanation.foundation:
Include two compact claims in every 10-minute access JWT:
- **`jti` (Token ID)**: Enables surgical revocation of a single compromised device/session.
explanation.core: - **`ver` (User Security Epoch)**: A monotonically increasing integer per user.
explanation.deepDive: On password reset or account takeover, incrementing `ver` in one record invalidates *all* outstanding access and refresh tokens for that user without enumerating every `jti`.

decisionFramework.problem: How to implement Design a Multi-Region Session & Token Revocation Service without hitting unbounded tail latency, state divergence, or operational fragility.
decisionFramework.naiveSolution: Use a single unpartitioned path with unbounded retries and synchronous global coordination.
decisionFramework.whyItFails: Global coordination serializes throughput under load, while unbounded retries amplify transient stalls into full outages.
decisionFramework.alternatives: Compare synchronous strict-consistency paths against bounded asynchronous replication, local caching, or partitioned ownership.
decisionFramework.decision: If latency budgets leave no room for synchronous retries, never make synchronous cross-region database calls on every API request; keep the hot read path in edge memory and bound the revocation window with short JWT TTLs + fast push invalidation.
decisionFramework.tradeOffs: Gains predictable p99 latency and fault isolation in exchange for explicit bounding, observability, and slightly higher implementation complexity.

decisionExercise.prompt: When Design a Multi-Region Session & Token Revocation Service experiences a sudden 5x traffic spike alongside a slow downstream dependency, which engineering choice best protects system stability?

options.label: Increase retry counts and remove client timeouts so every request eventually succeeds.
options.explanation: Unbounded retries multiply load on an already struggling dependency and exhaust worker pools.

options.label: Enforce strict latency budgets, bounded jittered retries, and graceful fallback or load shedding.
options.explanation: Bounding retries and isolating slow paths preserves healthy capacity and keeps tail latency predictable.

learningJourney.title: Sub-2 ms Edge Verification via Local Filter + Regional Redis
learningJourney.purpose: Keep 99.9%+ of API requests off the network using in-memory edge filters and fail-closed/fail-open risk tiers.

explanation.foundation: Each Edge Gateway maintains an in-memory map of `(revoked_jti -> exp)` and `(user_id -> min_valid_epoch)` synced via streaming deltas from its regional Redis cluster:
explanation.core:
1. Verify JWT signature locally with cached JWKS.
2. Check local in-memory filter (`O(1)`, `< 50 µs`).
3. If the edge filter is stale (`last_sync_age > 5s`), fall back to Regional Redis for high-risk endpoints (payments, password change) while allowing low-risk reads if configured.
explanation.deepDive: In production deployments of Design a Multi-Region Session & Token Revocation Service, watch how sub-2 ms edge verification via local filter + regional redis interacts with tail latency, retry amplification, and partial failures. 2M RPS multi-region revocation architecture: `jti` + monotonic `epoch` claims, sub-2 ms edge filters, Lua monotonic guards, skew-buffered TTLs, and partition fail-closed tiers.

learningJourney.title: Authoritative Store, Cross-Region Stream & Push Invalidation
learningJourney.purpose: Propagate revocations globally in under 5 seconds using durable writes + async fan-out + periodic anti-entropy.

explanation.foundation: When a user revokes a session or resets their password:
explanation.core:
1. **Authoritative Write**: Update the multi-region DB (or revoke refresh token family) transactionally.
2. **Publish Event**: Emit `{ type: 'REVOKE_JTI' | 'BUMP_EPOCH', id, ttl }` to a cross-region replicated stream (e.g., Kafka MirrorMaker / DynamoDB Streams).
3. **Regional Fan-Out**: Workers in all 4 regions write to Regional Redis (`SETEX` with remaining JWT TTL) and push via pub/sub to Edge Gateways.
explanation.deepDive: In production deployments of Design a Multi-Region Session & Token Revocation Service, watch how authoritative store, cross-region stream & push invalidation interacts with tail latency, retry amplification, and partial failures. 2M RPS multi-region revocation architecture: `jti` + monotonic `epoch` claims, sub-2 ms edge filters, Lua monotonic guards, skew-buffered TTLs, and partition fail-closed tiers.

learningJourney.title: Handling Cross-Region Partitions & Refresh Token Rotation
learningJourney.purpose: Combine refresh-token reuse detection with fail-closed sensitive endpoints during regional isolation.

explanation.foundation: Think of **Handling Cross-Region Partitions & Refresh Token Rotation** as the intuition layer for Design a Multi-Region Session & Token Revocation Service: Combine refresh-token reuse detection with fail-closed sensitive endpoints during regional isolation.
explanation.core:
- **Refresh Token Reuse Detection**: Refresh tokens are always validated against the authoritative store; if a rotated/revoked refresh token is replayed, immediately bump the user's `epoch`.
- **Partition Mode**: If a region loses stream connectivity (`sync_lag > 10s`), high-risk endpoints (`/transfer`, `/password`) fail closed to the authoritative store while non-sensitive reads stay available.
explanation.deepDive: Under heavy load or partial failure, handling cross-region partitions & refresh token rotation becomes a critical lever for predictable latency and correctness. 2M RPS multi-region revocation architecture: `jti` + monotonic `epoch` claims, sub-2 ms edge filters, Lua monotonic guards, skew-buffered TTLs, and partition fail-closed tiers.

learningJourney.title: Clock Skew, Out-of-Order Epochs & Cache Stampedes
learningJourney.purpose: Mitigate JWT clock-skew leaks, epoch regressions, and JWKS rotation thundering herds.

explanation.foundation: - **Clock Skew**: Add a 30–60s buffer to revocation `SETEX` TTLs so a token accepted by a slightly skewed edge clock cannot slip past an expired deny entry.
explanation.core: - **Out-of-Order Events**: Always compare `new_epoch > current_epoch` atomically in Redis Lua.
explanation.deepDive: - **JWKS Stampedes**: Cache JWKS with background refresh + jitter rather than synchronous fetch on unknown `kid`.

beginner.summary: Use short-lived login tokens plus a fast in-memory deny list at each edge server so stolen tokens are blocked within seconds.
beginner.keyTakeaway: If latency budgets leave no room for synchronous retries, never make synchronous cross-region database calls on every API request; keep the hot read path in edge memory and bound the revocation window with short JWT TTLs + fast push invalidation.
beginner.byteSummary:
If a login token lasts for weeks, logging out won't stop a hacker who copied it. Instead, apps give out short 10-minute tokens and keep a small in-memory list of recently revoked tokens at each edge gateway.

When someone logs out or resets their password, a central service saves the change and pushes the update to every region in a couple of seconds.

intermediate.summary: Combine 10-minute JWTs (`jti` + `ver` epoch) with `< 2 ms` edge in-memory filters, regional Redis fallback, and async cross-region push invalidation.
intermediate.keyTakeaway: If latency budgets leave no room for synchronous retries, never make synchronous cross-region database calls on every API request; keep the hot read path in edge memory and bound the revocation window with short JWT TTLs + fast push invalidation.
intermediate.byteSummary:
Edge gateways validate JWT signatures locally and check `(jti, user_epoch)` against an in-memory revocation filter synced from Regional Redis (`< 2 ms` p99).

Revocations write to an authoritative multi-region store and stream via async fan-out workers (with bounded retry + DLQ) to all regions within 5 seconds, expiring automatically once the JWT's `exp` passes.

advanced.summary: 2M RPS multi-region revocation architecture: `jti` + monotonic `epoch` claims, sub-2 ms edge filters, Lua monotonic guards, skew-buffered TTLs, and partition fail-closed tiers.
advanced.keyTakeaway: If latency budgets leave no room for synchronous retries, never make synchronous cross-region database calls on every API request; keep the hot read path in edge memory and bound the revocation window with short JWT TTLs + fast push invalidation.
advanced.byteSummary:
With 2M RPS reads and a 5s global revocation SLA, synchronous cross-region DB reads are infeasible. Short-lived JWTs (10m TTL) cap active deny-list state to ~3M entries (~100 MB), while `jti` + monotonic `ver` epoch claims handle both single-device and global logouts in O(1).

Edge gateways check local filters (`< 50 µs`) and fall back to Regional Redis or authoritative DB on stale syncs for sensitive routes. Regional workers use atomic Lua `new_epoch > cur_epoch` guards, skew-buffered `SETEX` TTLs, and bounded backoff + DLQ.

prerequisites.title: Passkeys, WebAuthn & FIDO2 Passwordless Auth
prerequisites.summary: WebAuthn/FIDO2 replaces passwords with per-site asymmetric keypairs generated inside a user's hardware authenticator, where private keys never leave the device and signatures are cryptographically bound to the exact Relying Party origin.

prerequisites.title: API Security: OAuth 2.1, JWT & mTLS
prerequisites.summary: Modern API security pairs OAuth 2.0 (for delegated user/client authorization), signed JWTs (for stateless, verifiable claims), and Mutual TLS (mTLS) (for cryptographic workload and high-assurance client identity).

prerequisites.title: JWT Validation Pitfalls & Hardening (RFC 8725)
prerequisites.summary: Stateless JSON Web Tokens fail catastrophically when verifiers trust header fields (`alg`, `kid`, `jku`), skip audience/issuer checks, or confuse asymmetric public keys with HMAC secrets.
